lesson.title: Significant Doesn't Always Mean It Matters
lesson.summary: A relationship can be statistically significant, very unlikely to be chance, while still being practically insignificant, too small in magnitude to matter, especially when the sample size is enormous.
lesson.body:
Statistical significance and practical significance answer genuinely different questions, and it's entirely possible for a result to be one without the other. Statistical significance, a small p-value, is about confidence that an effect isn't exactly zero. Practical significance is about whether that effect is big enough to matter to an actual person, patient, business, or policy decision. The danger is that statistical significance gets easier to achieve as sample size grows, even for an effect so small it's practically irrelevant, because SE(b1) = s / sqrt(SSxx) shrinks as more data is added (SSxx tends to grow as x-values accumulate), which inflates t = b1 / SE(b1) for any fixed, nonzero b1, however small.

Here is a hypothetical example, clearly a made-up illustration rather than a citation to any real study, built to make the danger concrete and checkable. Imagine a health-tracking company runs a regression predicting resting heart rate (in beats per minute) from height (in inches) across a huge sample of 500,000 adult users. Suppose the fitted slope comes out to b1 = −0.05 bpm per inch of height (taller people have a marginally lower average resting heart rate), with a standard error of SE(b1) = 0.006, tiny because the sample is enormous. The test statistic is t = −0.05 / 0.006 ≈ −8.33, with df ≈ 499,998. A t-statistic of that size, at that many degrees of freedom, gives a p-value far below 0.0001, an overwhelming statistical significance by any conventional standard.

Now check whether it's practically significant. Going from a 5-foot-tall person to a 6-foot-tall person is a 12-inch difference, and this slope predicts a heart rate difference of just 12 × 0.05 = 0.6 beats per minute. Resting heart rate naturally varies by something like 10 beats per minute or more from one day to the next, just from activity, caffeine, sleep, or stress, so a predicted 0.6 bpm difference across a full foot of height is completely swamped by ordinary noise. It would never register as a meaningful signal on a wrist-worn heart rate monitor, or change any decision a doctor or patient would make. The effect size confirms the same story from a different angle: with a relationship this weak, R² here would be a small fraction of one percent, meaning essentially none of the person-to-person variation in heart rate is explained by height. Statistically real, yes. Practically irrelevant, also yes. Both are true about the exact same result at the exact same time.

The practical lesson: a large enough sample can make almost any nonzero effect look impressively significant, so reading 'p < 0.05' (or even p < 0.0001) is never the end of the analysis. The next question always has to be asked in the original, meaningful units of the problem: how big is this effect, really, and is it big enough to change what anyone would do? That's exactly why effect size gets reported alongside a p-value, never as a substitute for reporting it, in careful statistical work.

Contrast this deliberately with the hours-studied and quiz-score example running through this whole unit: there, b1 = 1.8 points per hour was both statistically significant (t ≈ 16.84, tiny p-value) and practically significant, R² = 98.6% and roughly an extra letter grade's worth of points for a few hours of studying is a difference any student or teacher would genuinely care about. Statistical significance isn't worthless, it's just answering a different question than practical significance, and a complete evaluation of any result has to ask both.
